items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The call opened 'Good afternoon, this is Joanna. How can I help?' and went straight to 'can you just verify your email address, please.' The customer never got a roadmap or a timeframe, and the only signpost came six minutes in — 'But I'll just explain to you how we work in our pricing as well.'
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up before starting the profile lookup.

Save Your Ass speech essentially absent — this is the largest single deduction on the call. The customer handed her the opening twice ('I'll just make sure to get as much done as I can', 'I'll try to [move] them myself as much as I can beforehand') and Joanna answered 'of course, of course, no problem. Whichever works for you.' No prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill framing, no consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls), and no 'take a carload' tip — on a move the customer herself described as 'literally a three minute drive,' where a carload tip is worth real money.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — she went straight to 'we do charge by the hour for all of our services.'

Disassembly/reassembly never mentioned as included, despite 'a queen size bed with the frame' being one of the two big items and three TVs needing unmounting. It was also never named as a time variable in the estimate.

What's-included list incomplete: 'two men and the truck... [wrap] to protect your furniture. The TV blanket [pads] shrink wraps... taxes, insurance, credit card fees' — gas, bands, and tools were never named.

Destination stairs never asked. The customer said the new place is 'townhouses' and Joanna probed floors only at the origin ('are they on the third floor... or everything's on the second floor'). She then named stairs as the key estimate driver without knowing the stair situation on the delivery end.
Never asked about additional rooms (garage, attic, balcony, storage unit), storage stops, or additional stops.

No 'reply with any corrections' and no BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email. The email was referenced only as a packing-update channel — 'respond to the email that I'll be sending you' — not as the customer's chance to verify move details.
Business hours and how to reach us never given; the close was only 'give us a call or you know, send us an email whichever works for you.'
60¢/lb baseline coverage never explained alongside No Worries, so the customer has no reference point for what the $2,000 is an upgrade from.

No Ecobox referral on a call where the customer twice raised her own materials ('and the packing [materials]. If I have boxes and everything, I just need help getting it done') — a natural, unmade referral.
No equivalents/reference framing (school-bus, truck-load) to help the customer picture the volume she described item by item.

Box count landed muddled: 'do you think you'll have about more than fifty boxes in total... or do you think you'll have more?' — an either/or that only offers 'more' — followed by '3035 does that sound a good number already at this time?' The number 30–35 was never cleanly restated or confirmed back.

Estimate padding not reconciled out loud. Joanna stated the typical range herself — 'this type of moves usually takes two and a half to three and a half hours to complete' — then quoted 'the four to five hour mark' for moving plus three hours of packing, an 8-hour / $1,590 booking on a one-bedroom load with easy parking and a three-minute drive. The $190 x 8 + $70 math is correct, but the jump above her own stated range was never justified to the customer.
top_strength: The middle of this call is close to textbook. The pricing and clock block was delivered nearly complete and in the right order — '$95 per hour per mover' with the day-of-week tier named ('if we will be doing your move on Tuesday this is actually our lowest hourly rate for the week'), the $190/hr two-mover math, the '$70' one-time travel fee called out as the only thing outside the hourly rate, and then all three differentiators back to back: 'no worries damage coverage. Which would give you up to $2,000 coverage for any repair replacement reimbursement,' 'meet your mover feature. Rest assured Linda we don't take daily contract... we'll send you their names ahead of time,' and 'on time guarantee if we run late, we provide discounts by the end of the day.' The clock section is a clean 4/4 — 'We will only start the time. Once we arrive at the pickup location, open the contract... There's just a two and a half hour minimum if we go over we only charge in fifteen minute increments. Does that make sense?' She also handled two genuine curveballs well: on the plants she gave an honest answer instead of a vague one ('we really don't cannot like put them [in] boxes... The guys may just need to ask you to sign a waiver'), and she offered a split-day option for the packing rather than forcing one shape ('we can just do a separate day probably pack the day before and then moving... the following day'). And the human moment was real: after the customer said 'it's a pretty hard move for me,' Joanna said 'I'm so sorry, I don't know what you're going through right now but I hope we can at least help you a little bit, you know, lift that stress out of you for this move.' That is the line that kept this customer on the phone. She closed the booking on the spot, accommodated the 9:00–9:30 window request, stated 'We don't take deposits,' and set her own follow-up for a week out.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: the Save Your Ass speech, worth 10 points and worth more than that in real move efficiency. The customer volunteered twice that she wanted to do work herself, and this is a three-minute drive with a partial-contents load — the single best Save Your Ass setup you will get. Joanna's answer was 'Whichever works for you, that's okay.' What she needed to say: 'Linda, here is how you keep this bill down. Everything you can consolidate before we get there makes the move shorter, and since you only pay for the time we use, that is money straight back to you. Get the loose stuff out of drawers and into boxes, get the photos off the walls, box up anything small and breakable, and stack it all in one room near the door. And because it is only a three-minute drive, take a carload yourself with the plants and anything small — those are the items that eat the most time for the least weight. Does that make sense?' That one paragraph pays for itself. Second priority: put the agenda at the top. 'Good afternoon, this is Joanna — may I get your name? Hi Linda, how are you today? Here is what I will do: I will gather the details on your move, then walk you through exactly how our pricing works and get you a real number. Takes about ten to fifteen minutes. Sound good?' She earned that customer's trust the hard way in the middle of the call when she could have had it in the first thirty seconds. Third: destination stairs. She named stairs as the one factor that matters for this estimate — 'the factor that we want to consider here are really the stairs' — while only knowing the origin layout, and the destination is a townhouse. One question: 'And at the new place, is that a two-story or three-story townhouse, and which floor are we carrying to?' Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-four review: Joanna stated the typical range as 2.5–3.5 hours and then booked 4–5 hours for the move plus 3 for packing. That is defensible on a job where the packing scope is genuinely unknown, and she said so, but it is exactly the conservative-padding pattern we are tracking — and she also told the customer she would 'block the whole truck' for eight hours. Watch the actual against the $1,590 when this move runs on 10/13; if it comes in near her own 2.5–3.5 hour range plus packing, the padding, not the reporting, is the problem. Also worth documenting: this is a 2,400 sqft three-story home, which normally routes to a virtual walkthrough, and she quoted it directly off an item list because it is a one-bedroom partial move. That was the right call — but it should be noted on the job so nobody downstream reads a 2,400 sqft quote as a full-house estimate.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and accommodating — used 'Linda' four times, met the customer's implied hardship with real empathy ('I hope we can at least help you a little bit, you know, lift that stress out of you'), and flexed on the arrival window without friction, though the delivery is padded with heavy 'Mm-hmm' filler and several sentences that run on and lose their thread.
audio_review_reason: Several load-bearing numbers come through the transcript garbled — '3035 does that sound a good number,' 'twenty and a half hour minimum Smith,' 'no sterle fees,' '21904. Gan place in a place drive' — so whether the box count, the 2.5-hour minimum, the destination address, and the no-hidden-fees list were actually stated clearly to the customer cannot be judged from text alone.
